CO1: Start, pass arguments to, name, join and stop threads: Thread with target, args and kwargs, one start() per thread, join with and without a timeout, and the daemon flag set before start()
CO2: Explain why counter += 1 can lose updates when threads share it, repair the program with a Lock, and choose among Lock, RLock, Event, Semaphore and Queue, including how two locks taken in opposite orders deadlock
CO3: Run work on a ThreadPoolExecutor with map and submit, read a Future, and say when an exception, a timeout or a cancellation surfaces
CO4: Say when threads help and when they do not: waiting overlaps on any build, CPU-bound work gains nothing on the standard build with the global interpreter lock and does on the free-threaded build, and processes and asyncio are the alternatives
CO5: Judge what a threading result is worth: which timings are single runs on 2 CPUs, which builds and platforms were not run, and what a browser's Python can and cannot do with threads
_note: Threads (file slot 25) teaches the multithreading of the 2nd edition's chapter 17, which the 3rd edition dropped. The course's approved outcomes are not claimed to be served by these chapter objectives; attaching one is the owner's decision.
